    DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
  PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

        Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc., (“Meta”) by and through its undersigned counsel, hereby

respectfully opposes Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine’s Motion for Leave to File a Second Amended

Complaint pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d), Dkt. No. 59. Meta hereby joins,

adopts and incorporates all applicable arguments and requested relief contained in Defendants

Katie Hall and National Center for Missing & Exploited Children’s (“NCMEC Defendants”)

Opposition to Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File a Second Amended Complaint (Dkt. No. 74). In

further support, Meta states as follows:

   I.      Procedural History

        As described in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), Plaintiff

has filed a series of actions against Meta across several different courts, all stemming from the

alleged disablement of his Facebook account. See Dkt. No. 22 at 3-5. Across all of these actions,

Plaintiff has routinely filed amended complaints (or sought leave to do so), consistently delaying



                                                1

decision on motions to dismiss across those actions. Indeed, since September 9, 2025 (when

Plaintiff filed his first complaint against Meta in the United States District Court for the Northern

District of California), Plaintiff has filed 12 distinct complaints against Meta across four different

courts.

          Plaintiff’s present request for leave to amend continues his strategy of seeking repeated

amendments to delay decision on motions to dismiss. Indeed, in this court alone, Plaintiff has:

             •   Filed a complaint based on the allegations raised in the FAC against NCMEC and
                 Defendant Katie Hall (together, the “NCMEC Defendants) in a distinct action
                 (Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children, No. 1:26-cv-1341 (E.D.
                 Va.);
             •   Filed a motion for leave to amend that complaint to add claims against Meta;
             •   Voluntarily dismissed that action after the NCMEC Defendants opposed his request
                 for leave to amend;
             •   Filed the complaint and FAC against the NCMEC Defendants and Meta in the
                 instant action; and
             •   Following motions to dismiss, filed a motion for leave to file supplement his
                 pleading, withdrew that motion, and filed the instant motion for leave to amend.

See Dkt. No. 22 at 5; Dkt. No. 57; Dkt. No. 59.

   II.       Plaintiff’s Supplemental Allegations are Futile

          “[T]he standards used by a district court in ruling on a motion to amend or on a motion to

supplement [a complaint] are nearly identical.” Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d 184, 198, n. 15 (4th Cir.

2002). In either case, “leave to amend a pleading should be denied. . . when the amendment would

be futile.” Brannen v. Selene Finance, LP, No. 2:18-cv-602, 2019 WL 13251099, at *2, 5 (E.D.

Va. Nov. 14, 2019) (denying leave to file supplemental complaint where “it would be futile to

permit” Plaintiff’s “supplemental pleading” where his “right to relief” remained “a matter of pure

speculation”).




                                                  2

As to Plaintiff’s supplemental allegations regarding the NCMEC Defendants, Meta fully

adopts the arguments in NCMEC’s Opposition, which explain why the supplemental allegations

are “futile,” “unnecessary,” and a further attempt to prolong the litigation. Dkt. No. 74 at 4-5.

          As to Plaintiff’s supplemental allegations regarding Meta, Plaintiff seeks to add allegations

that in a motion to dismiss in a separate action brought by Plaintiff (Ballentine v. Meta Platforms,

Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.)), Meta described Plaintiff’s litigation against the

NCMEC Defendants as one of several actions Plaintiff has brought arising from the alleged

disablement of his Facebook account. See Dkt. No. 60 at 9. Plaintiff asserts that Meta’s citation

there of the present action is “a subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s knowledge, state of mind, and

awareness of the relationship between the two proceedings.” Id.

          But Meta’s knowledge, as of August 13, 2026, that Plaintiff sued NCMEC has no relevance

whatsoever to Plaintiff’s claims against Meta. Those claims are premised on Plaintiff’s assertion

that Meta somehow conspired with NCMEC in connection with letters that NCMEC sent to

Plaintiff on April 22, 2026. Plaintiff’s proffered supplemental allegations regarding Meta’s

knowledge of Plaintiff’s suit against NCMEC are plainly irrelevant to Plaintiff’s claims against

Meta or the issues raised in Meta’s motion to dismiss. Therefore, amendment would be futile and

Plaintiff’s motion should be denied. See Dacha v. Moody, No. 3:24-cv-713, 2026 WL 625494, at

*15 (E.D. Va. Mar. 5, 2026) (denying motion to supplement under Rule 15(d) because

supplementation with allegations that could not plausibly serve “as a factual basis for any claim”

against defendants “would be futile”).

   III.      Conclusion

          For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court deny Plaintiff’s Motion

for Leave to File a Second Amended Complaint.
